concepts.summary: How Linux splits the superuser's power into separate privileges, such as binding to a low port, that can be granted one at a time.

Linux splits root's power into separate units called capabilities, which can be granted and dropped one at a time.

concepts.summary: How Linux organizes processes into a hierarchy of groups whose CPU, memory and other resource use can be limited and measured.

sources.sections: DESCRIPTION; Terminology; Cgroups version 1 and version 2; Creating cgroups and moving processes; CGROUPS VERSION 2; Cgroups v2 controllers; Cgroups v2 subtree control; FILES

inlines.v: Control groups, usually called cgroups, let the kernel organize processes into a tree of groups and then limit and measure the resources each group uses: CPU time, memory, I/O, the number of processes, and more.
The parts that do the limiting are

There are two versions. Version 1 let each controller have its own separate hierarchy. Version 2, official since Linux 4.5, puts every controller in one unified hierarchy, and is meant to replace version 1, which remains for compatibility.

concepts.title: Character encoding and UTF-8
concepts.summary: How text is stored as bytes, from 7-bit ASCII through the ISO 8859 sets to UTF-8, and why one byte is not always one character.

sources.sections: DESCRIPTION; Properties; Encoding; Application notes; Security

inlines.v: Text in a file is a sequence of bytes; an

ASCII is the original 7-bit code: 128 characters covering English letters, digits, punctuation and control codes such as newline and tab.

has the full table in octal, decimal and hexadecimal. The ISO/IEC 8859 family, such as Latin-1, kept ASCII as the lower half and used the upper half for the letters of one group of languages at a time.
Unicode aims to give every character in every language its own number, and UTF-8 is the common way to store it on Unix-like systems:

items.v: ASCII characters are stored as the same single bytes, so a pure ASCII file is already valid UTF-8.
Every other character takes two to four bytes, all of them 0x80 or above, so no byte inside a multibyte character can be mistaken for
or the null byte. The copyright sign © is stored as
The first byte tells how long the sequence is, so a reader can resynchronize after damaged data.

inlines.v: Programs learn the encoding from the

. In a UTF-8 locale a single byte is not necessarily a single character, and one character does not always take one column on screen: wide East Asian characters take two, and combining marks take none.
Each character must use its shortest encoding, and programs must reject longer forms, which could slip a
past checks for the ASCII byte.

concepts.title: Namespaces
concepts.summary: How Linux gives a group of processes its own isolated view of a global resource, such as process IDs, mounts or the network; the basis of containers.

sources.sections: DESCRIPTION; Namespace types; The namespaces API; The /proc/pid/ns/ directory

inlines.v: A namespace wraps a global system resource so that the processes inside it appear to have their own private copy. Changes made inside are visible to the other members of the namespace and invisible to everyone else. Combining several namespaces is how containers are built.
Linux has eight types, each isolating one resource:

items.v: : the mount points, so a process can see a different file tree.

: the host name and NIS domain name.
: System V IPC objects and POSIX message queues.
: user and group IDs and capabilities, so a process can have user ID 0 inside while it is an ordinary user outside.

inlines.v: Every process belongs to one namespace of each type, and a child starts in its parent's.

Permission bits come in three groups of three: read, write and execute. The kernel uses the owner's group if the process's effective user ID owns the file, the group's if the file's group is one of the process's groups, and otherwise the last. For a directory,
means permission to search it, which is why a directory you cannot search blocks every path through it.
Root traditionally bypasses these checks. On Linux that power comes from the
